## From medicine soup to monastery to tea room

The packs describe a pathway in plain words: medicinal drink (Han) → focus aid in Chan/Zen monasteries (Tang/Song) → highly ritualized social practice (Japan's *chado*). Cultural historians such as James Benn trace how tea moved through Chinese religious and medical worlds before it became a global grocery staple [^1].

**Han & Tang (about 206 BC–907 AD).** Early tea was often a bitter soup with salt, ginger, peel, scallions. Medical texts such as the *Shennong Ben Cao Jing* tradition list it for food poisoning, liver tonic use, and clearing "brain fog" (pack summary of that medical-era framing).

**Tang & Song monasteries (about 618–1279).** Chan monks used tea to stay awake in long meditation without relying on harsher stimulants. Communal codes eventually wrote tea into the daily timetable.

**Japan from Eisai onward (from 1191).** Eisai promoted tea; later tea rooms used *ichigo ichie* ("one time, one meeting"). Status was leveled on the tatami—useful for serious talks [^2][^3].

First tea is "medicine soup." Later it is "stay awake for long practice." Still later it is "a shared room with rules that make everyone equal for a while." Same leaf family, different human jobs.

| When | Text / practice | What it did | Source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1103 | *Chanyuan Qinggui* (Chan monastic code) | Formal communal tea before dawn practice; seating and bowl rules | Yifa (2002; pack) |
| 1211 | Eisai's *Kissa Yōjōki* | Tea as nourishment; bitter flavor said to nourish the heart and curb lethargy | Eisai (1211); Sen (1998) [^2] |
| About 760 | Lu Yu's *Cha Jing* | Three boils by bubble look: "fish eyes," "pearls," "billowing waves" | Lu Yu; Carpenter (1974; pack) |
| 1906 | Okakura Kakuzō, *The Book of Tea* | A modern English-language window onto tea aesthetics for Western readers | Okakura (1906) [^4] |

Ritual and focus uses of tea are old. Modern "calm alertness" talk sits beside a long cultural history—not instead of it.

And because folklore loves a dramatic birth story: Bodhidharma's eyelids grew into tea bushes, people say. That is popular folklore, not early Chan history. The story is missing from early Chinese Chan collections (for example the *Records of the Transmission of the Lamp*, 1004). It shows up much later in Jesuit travel writing and late-Edo Japanese popular books (pack historiography note).

Eisai's 1211 phrase about tea nourishing the heart sits, in the packs, beside modern findings that tea compounds can raise calming parasympathetic (HRV) tone. That is a historical phrase meeting a modern measure—not proof that Eisai ran an HRV lab. (See [Linkages](../../linkages.qmd).)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="More detail: from medicine soup to Chan code to chado"}
| When | Text / practice | What it did | Trail |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ~760 | Lu Yu's *Cha Jing* | Three boils by bubble look: "fish eyes," "pearls," "billowing waves" | Lu Yu; Carpenter (1974; pack) |
| 1103 | *Chanyuan Qinggui* | Formal communal tea before dawn practice; seating and bowl rules | Yifa (2002; pack) |
| 1211 | Eisai's *Kissa Yōjōki* | Tea as nourishment; bitter flavor said to nourish the heart and curb lethargy | Eisai; Sen (1998)[^2][^3] |
| 1906 | Okakura, *The Book of Tea* | Modern English-language window onto tea aesthetics for Western readers | Okakura (1906)[^4] |

Pathway in plain words: medicinal drink (Han) → focus aid in Chan/Zen monasteries (Tang/Song) → highly ritualized social practice (Japan's *chado*).[^1] Early tea was often a bitter soup with salt, ginger, peel, scallions. Later, monks used tea to stay awake in long meditation without harsher stimulants. In Japan, *ichigo ichie* ("one time, one meeting") and tatami etiquette leveled status for serious talks.[^2][^3]

**Folklore check.** "Bodhidharma's eyelids grew into tea bushes" is popular folklore, not early Chan history—it is missing from early Chinese Chan collections such as the *Records of the Transmission of the Lamp* (1004) and shows up much later in Jesuit travel writing and late-Edo popular books (pack historiography note).
:::

From monasteries we step into a quieter modern lab: what happens when you simply *hold* a warm cup?



::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="More detail: reading the timetable without romance"}
The monastic codes and Eisai's essay are **prescriptions and promotions**, not lab notebooks. *Chanyuan Qinggui* (1103) shows tea written into a communal schedule; *Kissa Yōjōki* (1211) argues for tea as nourishment against lethargy; Lu Yu's *Cha Jing* teaches attention to the boil by eye.[^1][^2]

What the packs do *not* claim: that every modern cafe ritual descends unbroken from Chan, or that *ichigo ichie* causes cooperation in Trust Games. Those are later bridges on [Linkages](../../linkages.qmd)—historical phrase beside modern measure—not proof that monks ran EEG labs.
:::
